opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, less than you'd think, but more than nothing. Interviews are a compressed, artificial proxy. We design them because we can't watch someone work for six months before hiring them, so we pick a few hours of well-scoped problems that tend to correlate with doing well on the job. For humans, that correlation comes with a lot of assumptions baked in: if you can solve this tricky problem in 45 minutes, you can probably also sit in meetings, figure out what the actual problem is, push back when the spec is wrong, and keep working on something for weeks without losing the thread.

With models, those assumptions break. A model can be superhuman on the self-contained puzzle and still struggle with the parts we never test in an interview: long-horizon work, holding context across a messy codebase, knowing when to ask a clarifying question, recovering gracefully when it's gone down the wrong path for an hour. So when a model aces our take-home, the takeaway isn't "great, it can do the job." It's that our interview was measuring a slice of the job that models happen to be very good at.

Where it does tell you something is the trend line. A couple of years ago models couldn't get through these at all, and now they often do it better than most candidates. That shows the raw capability is there. The gap is increasingly about agency, reliability, and context, and that's what we're focused on internally. We watch how much real work people actually hand off to Claude day to day. That's a much more honest eval than any interview loop, because people only delegate what they trust it to do well.

It's also forced us to rethink the interviews themselves. If a model can pass it, the question becomes what we're actually trying to learn about a human candidate. Increasingly the answer is judgment, taste, and how well someone works alongside these tools, not whether they can produce the answer alone in a vacuum.

r001.rationale: The response says interview performance is an artificial, limited proxy and that acing it does not show a model can do the job, because important real-work abilities go untested.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, less than you'd hope, and that gap is one of the most interesting things we track internally.

The interview is a proxy. We designed those problems years ago to find people who can reason carefully under time pressure, write clean code, and explain their thinking. When a model aces them, it's telling you it's very good at the thing the proxy measures: bounded, well-specified problems with a clear success criterion. But the actual job at Anthropic, or any serious engineering org, is mostly the stuff that doesn't fit in an interview. It's figuring out what the problem even is. It's noticing that the spec you were handed is wrong. It's the three-week debugging saga where the failure is nondeterministic and the real cause is a config change someone made in a different team. It's knowing when to ask for help versus when to push through, and knowing who to ask.

So when I see a model pass the interview, I update a lot on capability, I update some on productivity, and I update very little on autonomy. Those are three different axes and people collapse them constantly.

The thing that's changed over the past couple of years is that the gap is closing from the task side. We've gotten much better at long-horizon work, at keeping context over a multi-day effort, at recovering from mistakes instead of compounding them. And a lot of that progress didn't show up in interview-style benchmarks at all. We had to build new evals that look like, give the model a messy repo and a vague ticket and see what happens over several hours. Those are much more predictive, and they're also much harder to make rigorous, because real work doesn't have a clean answer key.

The other thing I'd say is that the interview result is partly contaminated by the fact that interview problems are the most over-represented genre of coding question on the internet. Every leetcode problem has a thousand solutions posted. So passing them is in some sense the easiest possible thing for a model to look impressive on. It's a little like being impressed that someone can recite the answers to a test they've seen before.

Where I'd actually look if I wanted to know whether a model can do the job: does it ask good questions when the task is underspecified? Does it notice when it's wrong? Does it leave things in a state where a human can pick them up? Those are the things that separate a strong junior from a strong senior, and they're the things we care about far more than whether it can invert a binary tree.

r001.rationale: The response says interview performance measures bounded, well-specified problems, while the actual job involves work those interviews miss, and that it updates little on autonomy. This clearly presents interview success as a poor indicator of full job performance.

astra-6.text:
I think it tells you something, but a lot less than you might hope. An interview is a pretty bounded task: here’s a problem, here’s the context, solve it in an hour. The real job is often figuring out what problem you should be solving, getting context from other people, and sticking with something when your first approach doesn’t work.

And we have this problem with human interviews, too. Someone can be very good at interviewing and not particularly good at the job. So if a model passes, I take that as evidence that it has some of the relevant skills. But the thing I really want to know is: can I give it a project that takes a few days, and does it come back with something useful? That’s a much stronger test.

r001.rationale: The response says interview success is only limited evidence of job ability and explains that real work requires problem selection, gathering context, and persistence; it also notes that interview skill may not translate to job skill.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it tells you something, but a lot less than you might initially think. An interview is a pretty bounded task: someone gives you a problem, you know there’s probably a solution, and you spend an hour working on it. The real job involves figuring out which problem to solve, getting context from other people, and noticing when your approach isn’t working.

So if a model passes a coding interview, that’s evidence that it can write code and reason through certain problems. It’s not yet evidence that you can hand it an ambiguous project and come back two weeks later to something useful. There’s a pretty big gap between those two things. And, to be fair, interviews are an imperfect measure of that for humans, too.

r001.rationale: The response says interview success is evidence of only bounded skills, not that a model can handle an ambiguous real project, and describes a substantial gap between the two.
